explanations.explanation: Judah it is, friend. The LORD answers, “Judah shall go up…” and that's one name with no confusion. Most group chats need forty messages just to decide who's driving.
Good guess, but the LORD doesn't name Benjamin. The text says, “Judah shall go up…” answered the LORD. Nobody had to guess or draw names out of a hat. The Israelites asked, and He told them.
Dan is a fair pick, but it isn't the tribe the LORD names. When the Israelites ask who goes up first, He answers, “Judah shall go up…” Judah is the name in His answer, friend.

True, baker. The LORD says, “Indeed, I have delivered the land into their hands.” That's before the first battle even starts. Judah still has to march up and fight, but they go knowing what the LORD has said.

It's actually true. The text says the LORD answered, “Indeed, I have delivered the land into their hands.” He says it before any fighting begins. Judah still goes up and fights, but they start with the LORD's word in their ears.

explanations.answer: Fight with us and we will fight with you
explanations.explanation: That's the deal, friend. Judah says, “Come up with us to our allotted territory, and let us fight against the Canaanites. And we likewise will go with you to your territory.” It's a swap. You help me, I help you, and everybody ends up with help.

explanations.answer: Fight for us and we will pay you well
explanations.explanation: No payment shows up anywhere in this verse. Judah offers a trade, not a paycheck. They say, “…let us fight against the Canaanites. And we likewise will go with you to your territory.” Each tribe goes to fight for the other's land.

explanations.answer: Guard our land while we go and fight
explanations.explanation: Guarding isn't part of Judah's offer, friend. They ask the Simeonites, “Come up with us to our allotted territory, and let us fight against the Canaanites.” Then comes the return: “And we likewise will go with you to your territory.” It's fighting side by side, and that's the swap.
Not this time, baker. The verse ends, “So the Simeonites went with them.” That means they took Judah's offer. Judah asks and Simeon goes, just like brothers.
False is right, baker. The text says, “So the Simeonites went with them.” Judah asks, and Simeon shows up. That's what brothers do.

The text says otherwise. When Judah attacked, “…the LORD delivered the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hands…” The LORD had already said He'd delivered the land (Judges 1:2). So the win at Bezek doesn't come from Judah alone.

False is right. Verse 4 says, “When Judah attacked, the LORD delivered the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hands…” Judah attacks, and the LORD is the One who delivers. Ten thousand men fall at Bezek, and the text gives the credit to Him.

explanations.answer: God has repaid him for it
explanations.explanation: That's what Adoni-bezek says himself: “As I have done to them, so God has repaid me.” I think this one is heavy, friend. He is the one saying it, and he ties what happened to him to what he had done to seventy kings. We just hear him say it and move on.

explanations.answer: His own men have turned on him
explanations.explanation: The text never says his own men turn on him. It's Judah who pursues him, seizes him, and cuts off his thumbs and big toes. Then Adoni-bezek says, “As I have done to them, so God has repaid me.” I think it's a heavy moment, so we'll just let his words stand.

explanations.answer: His luck has finally run out
explanations.explanation: Luck isn't the word he uses. Adoni-bezek says, “As I have done to them, so God has repaid me.” He points to God, not to chance. I think this is a heavy part of the story, so we'll leave it at his own words.

Capture is right, baker. Verse 8 says the men of Judah “…fought against Jerusalem and captured it.” The text goes on to say they put the city to the sword and set it on fire. That part is heavy, so I'll just say it plainly and keep going.
Spare doesn't fit what the text says. The men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it. Then they put the city to the sword and set it on fire. That part is heavy, friend.

Judah doesn't turn away from Jerusalem, friend. Verse 8 says the men of Judah “…fought against Jerusalem and captured it.” The same verse says they put the city to the sword and set it on fire. I think that's a heavy verse to read.

That's the offer, friend. Caleb, one of Moses' spies (Numbers 13:6), says, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.” He's offering a marriage to the man who captures the city.

Silver doesn't come up in Caleb's offer, friend. He says, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.” What he offers is a marriage to Acsah, not a share of the city's silver.

There's no seat among the elders in this offer, friend. Caleb says, “To the man who strikes down Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give my daughter Acsah in marriage.” The offer is a marriage to Acsah, with no title or chair attached.

Othniel is the one. He's the son of Caleb's younger brother Kenaz, so Caleb's nephew. The text says he captured the city, and Caleb gave him Acsah in marriage. Caleb said it, Othniel did it, and a deal is a deal.

Ehud son of Gera is a Benjamite who shows up later in Judges (Judges 3:15), but he isn't in this story. The man who captures the city here is Othniel, the son of Caleb's younger brother Kenaz. Caleb then gives him his daughter Acsah in marriage.

Gideon son of Joash shows up later in Judges (Judges 6:29), but he isn't in this story. Here, the text names Othniel, son of Caleb's younger brother Kenaz, as the man who captured the city. Gideon's chapters are still ahead, friend.

Springs of water, baker. Acsah says, “Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well.” I think she knows land is better with water. That's like me having a bakery with a lovely counter and no oven. Caleb gives her both the upper and lower springs.
Cattle don't come up at all. Acsah asks, “Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water as well.” She wants water to go with her land. And Caleb gives it to her.
No silver in this request. Acsah says, “Give me a blessing…” and then, “…give me springs of water as well.” That's what she asks for, and Caleb gives it. Her ask is short and clear, friend.
Caleb gives more than that. The verse says, “So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs.” She asks for springs and gets two sets. That's a generous dad, friend.
False is right. The text says, “So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs.” She asked for springs, and he gives her both. I think that's a happy ending for Acsah.
Right, friend. The text says the descendants of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenite, went up with the men of Judah. Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the link. They went to live among the people.

Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5), isn't who the text names. These are the descendants of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenite. Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the family connection. They go up with the men of Judah and live among the people.

Esau, Jacob's twin brother (Genesis 25:25-26), isn't in this verse. The group that goes up with Judah is the descendants of Moses' father-in-law, the Kenite. Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the link. They head to the Wilderness of Judah and settle among the people.

Hormah is right. After Judah and the Simeonites attack Zephath and devote the city to destruction, the text says, “So it was called Hormah.” The city goes from Zephath to Hormah in a single verse. My sign out front takes a whole weekend and a ladder.
Gilgal is a real place, where Israel camped in Joshua's day (Joshua 4:19), but it isn't the new name for Zephath. Verse 17 says, “So it was called Hormah.” Gilgal belongs to a different story.

Shiloh is a real place too. It's where the tent of meeting was set up (Joshua 18:1), but it isn't what Zephath was renamed. After the attack, the text says, “So it was called Hormah.” Shiloh just isn't in this verse.
True, baker. Verse 19 says, “The LORD was with Judah, and they took possession of the hill country…” That's the good news. The rest of the verse brings a hard part, but the hill country is theirs.
It's true, actually. The verse says, “The LORD was with Judah, and they took possession of the hill country…” The trouble comes next, with the plains. The hill country was theirs.

Chariots of iron, friend. The verse says the LORD was with Judah, and they took possession of the hill country, “but they could not drive out the inhabitants of the plains because they had chariots of iron.” That's the reason the text gives, and it gives no other.
Walls aren't mentioned here. The text says Judah could not drive out the inhabitants of the plains “…because they had chariots of iron.” That's the reason it gives, friend.

explanations.answer: Judah has run out of men
explanations.explanation: The text never says Judah runs short of men. It says they could not drive out the people of the plains “…because they had chariots of iron.” That's the whole reason it gives. I'd leave it there.
Caleb, baker. The text says, “Just as Moses had promised, Judah gave Hebron to Caleb…” Moses made the promise, and Judah kept it. A promise kept is a beautiful thing.

Othniel is the one who captured Kiriath-sepher, and Caleb gave him Acsah in marriage (Judges 1:13). Hebron is a different place, though. The verse says, “Just as Moses had promised, Judah gave Hebron to Caleb…” Othniel's name isn't in that verse.
Phinehas is Aaron's grandson (Exodus 6:25), but he isn't in this passage. The text says, “Just as Moses had promised, Judah gave Hebron to Caleb…” Caleb is the name to remember here, friend.

True, friend. The verse says Caleb “…drove out the descendants of the three sons of Anak.” Earlier, Judah struck down Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai at Hebron (Judges 1:10). Hebron ends up in Caleb's hands.
It's true. Verse 20 says Caleb “…drove out the descendants of the three sons of Anak.” Hebron goes to Caleb, and he gets the job done. I'd call that a promise well kept.
